engine.title: Help them say yes
engine.subtitle: Small daily moves that make treatment easier to say yes to — built on CRAFT, the most-studied approach for families of someone who refuses help.
engine.introTitle: Start with what you already know
engine.introBody: First you'll map their patterns: when use happens, what it gives them, what it's costing them, and when they're most reachable. Then the engine turns that into two small moves a day, a forecast of good moments, and words to invite them — in your own voice.
engine.evidence: In a well-known study (Miller, Meyers & Tonigan, 1999), about 2 in 3 families using CRAFT saw a loved one who refused help start treatment — roughly double a confrontational intervention. Nothing can promise that, but the odds are real, and families tend to feel better along the way.
engine.finishSetupBody: Choose whether you'd like a quiet heads-up when tonight may be a good window. Then your first two moves are ready.
engine.paywallBody: Membership unlocks the rest of the engine: two daily moves for your whole family, a receptivity forecast, invitation lines in your own words, and a simple record of what's working.

category.communication: Talk so they can hear it

reward_name_it.title: Name one sober moment out loud
reward_name_it.body: When you see them sober today — even for an hour — tell them what you noticed, right then. Be specific and leave it there: no “but,” no “finally.”
reward_name_it.example: “I really liked having coffee with you this morning. You were so present.”

reward_sober_plan.title: Make sober time the good time
reward_sober_plan.body: Plan one small thing they enjoy that only happens when they're sober: a favorite meal, a drive, a game, a show together. If they've been using, it quietly doesn't happen — no speech needed.
reward_sober_plan.example: “I'm making your chili tonight — want to eat together?”

reward_best_hour.title: Show up for their best hour
reward_best_hour.body: You know when they're most often sober and reachable. Be around then today — warm, unhurried, no agenda, and no talk about their use.
reward_best_hour.example: Sit with them during that time and talk about anything else.

reward_thank_effort.title: Thank the effort, right away
reward_thank_effort.body: If they skip a drink, come home on time, or keep a small promise, thank them within the minute. Small and specific beats big and late.
reward_thank_effort.example: “Thanks for calling to say you'd be late. That really helped me.”

reward_warm_moment.title: Let sober time feel good
reward_warm_moment.body: When they're sober, offer the kind of warmth that fits your relationship — a hug, a laugh, an inside joke. You're showing them what life without using can feel like.
reward_warm_moment.example: “It's really good to just hang out with you.”

step_back_when_using.title: Step away while they're using
step_back_when_using.body: If they're drinking or high today, calmly leave the room or end the call. No arguing, no lecture. Warmth comes back when they're sober.
step_back_when_using.example: “I'm going to head to bed. I'd love to talk tomorrow.”

let_it_land.title: Don't cushion one consequence
let_it_land.body: Pick one thing you usually fix after their use — a call to work, a mess, a late fee — and let it stay theirs today. Quietly, without announcing it.
let_it_land.example: Leave the bottles where they left them.

no_cover_story.title: Don't make the excuse
no_cover_story.body: If someone asks why they missed something, you don't have to cover for them — or explain. A simple, kind deflection is enough.

money_line.title: Hold the money line
money_line.body: If they ask for money today, you can say no warmly — or pay for something specific directly, like a bill or groceries, instead of handing over cash.
money_line.example: “I'm not going to give cash, but I'm happy to pick up groceries.”

morning_after.title: Let the morning after be theirs
morning_after.body: After a night of use, don't absorb the fallout — the missed alarm, the apologies to others, the cancelled plans. Be kind, and get on with your own day.
morning_after.example: “I hope you feel better. I've got errands — see you later.”

i_statement.title: Trade one “you” for an “I”
i_statement.body: Say how something affects you instead of what they did wrong. Start with “I feel” or “I love.” It's much harder to argue with.
i_statement.example: “I feel scared when you drive after drinking, because I love you.”

understanding.title: Say you understand one thing
understanding.body: Name something real about their side — the stress, the pain, how hard stopping seems. Understanding isn't agreeing.
understanding.example: “I know work has been brutal, and drinking feels like the only break you get.”

partial_responsibility.title: Own one small piece
partial_responsibility.body: Take responsibility for a small part of how past talks have gone. It lowers their guard without excusing their use.
partial_responsibility.example: “I know I've yelled when I was scared. I don't want to do that anymore.”

offer_help.title: Make an offer of help
offer_help.body: Offer something concrete and low-pressure that would make their life easier — and keep the door open for bigger help.
offer_help.example: “If you ever want to talk to someone, I'll find the right person and drive you.”

positive_request.title: Ask for what you want
positive_request.body: Turn one complaint into a clear, positive request. People can say yes to a request; they can only defend against a complaint.
positive_request.example: Instead of “Stop drinking every night,” try “Would you take a walk with me after dinner?”

listen_first.title: Listen for two minutes
listen_first.body: In one conversation today, just listen. Reflect back what you hear before you say anything about yourself.
listen_first.example: “Sounds like you feel like everyone's on your case.”

keep_it_short.title: Keep it under 30 seconds
keep_it_short.body: Pick one thing to say and say it briefly. Long talks feel like lectures, and lectures raise defenses.
keep_it_short.example: “I love you. I'm worried. I'm here.”

their_costs.title: Connect to what they care about
their_costs.body: Your pattern map lists costs they themselves have felt. If one comes up naturally, reflect it back gently — no “I told you so.”
their_costs.example: “You've seemed really down about things at work.”

answer_their_line.title: Have a calm answer ready
answer_their_line.body: Think of what they usually say when help comes up. Prepare one calm, short reply that doesn't argue — then let it go.
answer_their_line.example: “Maybe you're right. I just love you, and the offer's always open.”

pick_the_moment.title: Notice the open moments
pick_the_moment.body: Hard conversations go best when they're sober, calm and not rushed — and when you are too. Today, just notice when those moments happen.
pick_the_moment.example: Jot down one time today they seemed most open.

not_while_using.title: Never during or right after use
not_while_using.body: If they've been using, or they're hungover and irritable, it's not the time. Waiting isn't giving up — it's choosing the moment.

after_a_consequence.title: Be ready after something goes wrong
after_a_consequence.body: After a consequence — a ticket, a fight, a missed day — there's often a short window when they're more open. Stay calm and kind; skip the “I told you so.”
after_a_consequence.example: “That sounded awful. I'm here if you want help figuring it out.”

plan_around_trigger.title: Plan around one trigger
plan_around_trigger.body: Your pattern map names situations when use tends to happen. Plan something enjoyable during one of them — an alternative, not a confrontation.
plan_around_trigger.example: “Want to grab dinner Friday before the game?”

selfcare_one_thing.title: One thing just for you
selfcare_one_thing.body: Do one thing today that refills you — a walk, a call with a friend, a nap, a show. You're not being selfish; you're staying strong for the long haul.
selfcare_one_thing.example: Put 20 minutes on your calendar and protect it.

selfcare_support.title: Talk to someone on your side
selfcare_support.body: Reach out to one person who supports you — a friend, a group, your coach. You don't have to carry this alone.
selfcare_support.example: Text a friend, or join the Monday family call.

selfcare_sleep.title: Guard your sleep
selfcare_sleep.body: Don't wait up or check their phone tonight. Rest is part of the plan.
selfcare_sleep.example: “I'm going to bed. Text me when you're home.”

selfcare_good_thing.title: Notice one good thing in your life
selfcare_good_thing.body: Spend five minutes on something going right for you — a hobby, a friendship, work you're proud of. Your life matters beyond their use.
selfcare_good_thing.example: Write down one thing you're grateful for today.

selfcare_breathe.title: Breathe before you respond
selfcare_breathe.body: When you feel the urge to argue or plead, take three slow breaths first. A calm you is your strongest tool.
selfcare_breathe.example: In for 4, hold for 4, out for 6.

safety_plan.title: Make a safety plan
safety_plan.body: Decide where you'd go and who you'd call if things escalate: a room with a lock, a friend's house, your keys and phone where you can grab them.
safety_plan.example: Pack a small bag with ID, medications and a charger, and keep it somewhere safe.

safety_code_word.title: Choose a code word
safety_code_word.body: Agree on a word with someone you trust that means “call for help now.”
safety_code_word.example: Text your code word to a friend if you need them to call 911.

safety_talk_pro.title: Talk with a safety advocate first
safety_talk_pro.body: Before any conversation about treatment, talk it through with someone trained in safety planning. It's free and confidential.

safety_not_alone.title: Don't raise treatment alone
safety_not_alone.body: If you want to invite them to get help, do it only with a professional's guidance and other people present — never alone, and never while they're using.
safety_not_alone.example: Ask Matt or a counselor to help you plan it.

safety.title: Your safety comes first
safety.body: Because there has been violence, threats or fear, please don't invite them to treatment on your own. The engine won't suggest invitation windows. It will help you stay safe and plan the next step with a professional.
safety.danger: If you're in danger right now, call 911.
safety.hotlineTitle: National Domestic Violence Hotline — free, confidential, 24/7
safety.mattBody: Send Matt your situation. He'll help you work out a safe next step — including whether and how to raise treatment.

intro.title: Let's map their patterns
intro.body: CRAFT starts by understanding when use happens, what it does for them, and when they're most reachable. Use your own words — there are no wrong answers.
intro.note: About 10 minutes. We save as you go, so you can stop anytime.

safety.title: First, your safety
safety.body: When you've brought up their use, has there been violence, threats, or have you felt afraid?
safety.noneBody: Arguments maybe, but I've never felt unsafe.
safety.someBody: Yelling, slammed doors or broken things — I've felt uneasy.
safety.seriousBody: Hitting, threats, weapons, or I'm afraid of what they could do.
safety.someNote: Thank you for telling us. Keep conversations short, stay near an exit, and never talk while they're using. If that ever changes, update this answer.
safety.seriousNote: This changes only your plan: the engine won't suggest inviting them, won't send window alerts, and will focus on keeping you safe. Nobody in your family space is told, and their plans don't change.

triggers.title: When does use tend to happen?
triggers.body: Times, places, people or feelings — for example “Friday nights,” “after work with Dan,” or “after we argue.”

gives.title: What does using seem to give them?
gives.body: Not to excuse it — to understand it. Help works better when it offers something real in its place.

costs.title: What has it cost them — in their eyes?
costs.body: Costs they themselves have felt or complained about. These are the things they may want to change.

sober.title: When are they sober and reachable?
sober.body: The moments when a conversation could actually land.

phrases.title: What do they say when help comes up?
phrases.body: Their words, as close as you can remember. Conversation practice uses them so you can rehearse calm answers.

incidents.title: Anything recent you might mention?
incidents.body: Optional. One specific, recent moment you could gently refer to — said with care, never as evidence.
incidents.placeholder: e.g. missed Sam's game on Saturday

review.title: Here's your pattern map
review.body: Read it over. You can change anything later.

alerts.title: Would you like a heads-up?
alerts.body: When the forecast looks like a good window, we can send one discreet notification around 5 PM. On your lock screen it only says “You have a note for today” — open the app to see why. At most once every two days. You can turn it off anytime.

setup.doneBody: That's the hardest part of CRAFT done. Next: two small moves a day.

usualPhrases.canStop: I can stop whenever I want.
usualPhrases.onMyCase: Why are you always on my case?

kit.title: Get ready to ask
kit.body: Three things before you invite them: a next step that's ready, words that sound like you, and a quick warm-up.
kit.nextStepBody: A yes is fragile. Have one concrete next step lined up so it can happen today.
kit.noPlanBody: You don't have a program lined up yet. Find one first, so a yes can turn into a phone call right away.
kit.linesBody: Each one says: I love you, here's what I've noticed, would you get help, and I'll help you get there. Edit until it sounds like you.
kit.observationPlaceholder: e.g. you've seemed so tired after work
kit.personalize: Draft lines in my own words
kit.aiNote: Drafted from your pattern map. Edit freely.
kit.aiUnavailable: Couldn't draft new lines right now — these templates work well too.
kit.aiLimit: You've drafted a lot today. Use these templates, or edit your favorite.

style.help: Lead with your offer of help

kit.softenTip: Tip: leave out labels and “always/never” — they tend to raise defenses.
kit.warmupBody: A 90-second warm-up helps your voice stay steady when it counts.

tips.1: Choose a calm moment when they're sober — never while they're using or right after.
tips.2: Keep it short. Say your line, then listen.
tips.3: If they say no, stay warm: “Okay. The offer stands.” That's a seed, not a failure.
tips.4: If anything starts to feel unsafe, stop and step away.

not_yet.2: Keep the daily moves going. Reward every sober moment you see.

in_treatment.title: They're in treatment
in_treatment.body: The engine stops suggesting invitation windows while they're in treatment. Keep caring for yourself, and keep noticing and rewarding every sober step. If that changes, update their stage on Today.

after_yes.title: A yes was logged
after_yes.body: Someone in your family heard a yes, so invitation windows are paused for now. Keep the next steps steady with your Treatment Action Plan. If things change, log an update.

returning_home.title: They're coming home
returning_home.body: No more invitations needed for now. Focus on a calm homecoming: steady routines, clear boundaries, and noticing every sober step.

in_recovery.title: They're in recovery
in_recovery.body: The engine has stopped suggesting invitation windows. Keep rewarding the recovery you see and keep caring for yourself. If use returns, update their stage on Today and the engine will pick back up.

paused.updateStage: Their stage changed? Update it on Today

windowSafety.title: Something happened — stay safe first
windowSafety.body: A consequence can make people more open, but because you told us about violence or threats, please don't raise treatment on your own right now. Plan any next step with a professional.
windowSafety.unknownBody: We couldn't check your safety settings just now, so we're not suggesting what to say. If anything feels unsafe, don't raise treatment on your own.

crisis.title: Let's pause the invitation
crisis.body: What you wrote sounds like someone may be in danger — you, or them. Before any invitation, please reach out for real support. Nothing in your plan has changed; this is just for right now.
crisis.danger: If anyone is in danger right now, call 911. If they've talked about suicide, call or text 988.
